stem: Obligor A has a one-year PD of 10% and obligor B has a one-year PD of 15%. The probability that both default within the year is 3%. The default correlation between A and B is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 0.015 is the covariance, not yet divided by the product of standard deviations.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 0.122 divides the covariance by √(pA × pB), omitting the (1 − p) terms of the Bernoulli variances.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 0.280 divides the joint PD (0.03) rather than the covariance by the standard-deviation product.
rationale.D: Correct. Covariance of 0.015 divided by 0.1071 gives 0.140.

stem: A large, granular loan portfolio has total exposure of USD 50 million, PD of 2%, LGD of 45% and asset correlation of 0.20. Using the Vasicek one-factor model with N⁻¹(0.02) = −2.0537 and N⁻¹(0.999) = 3.0902, the 99.9% credit VaR (worst-case loss minus expected loss, USD millions) is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 5.09 is the worst-case loss (50 × 0.45 × 22.63%) without subtracting expected loss of 0.45.
rationale.B: Correct. WCDR of 22.63% less the 2% PD, times EAD × LGD of 22.5, gives USD 4.64 million.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 0.77 uses ρ instead of √ρ in the numerator, which drastically understates the WCDR.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 5.19 forgets to divide the argument by √(1 − ρ), overstating the WCDR.

stem: Holding PD, LGD and exposure constant, what is the effect of increasing the asset correlation in a Vasicek portfolio model?
options: Expected loss rises and the 99.9% worst-case default rate falls.
Both expected loss and the 99.9% worst-case default rate are unchanged.
Expected loss is unchanged, while the 99.9% worst-case default rate and credit VaR rise.
Expected loss falls because more borrowers survive together in good states.
explanation: Expected loss depends only on PD, LGD and EAD. Higher correlation makes defaults cluster, fattening the tail and raising the WCDR and credit VaR.

rationale.A: Incorrect. EL does not depend on correlation, and the tail default rate rises rather than falls.
rationale.B: Incorrect. The tail quantile is highly sensitive to correlation even though EL is not.
rationale.C: Correct. Correlation reshapes the loss distribution: same mean, fatter right tail.
rationale.D: Incorrect. The mean default rate stays at PD; clustering in good and bad states offsets in the average.

stem: A granular portfolio has exposure of USD 200 million, PD of 1.5% and LGD of 50%. A one-factor model gives a 99.9% worst-case default rate of 12%. The 99.9% credit VaR (USD millions) is closest to:

rationale.A: Correct. Worst-case loss of 12.0 less expected loss of 1.5 gives USD 10.5 million.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 12.0 is the worst-case loss before subtracting expected loss.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 24.0 applies the WCDR to the full exposure without LGD.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 1.5 is the expected loss, not the unexpected (VaR) amount.
